title: DCM syndicate desk question set
note: Bond syndicate, pricing, Schuldschein, hybrids, ratings and macro. Authored: the answers are parsed from the author's own desk handbook, where each is written as a script to say out loud, and the rubrics are written for this repo. Six items are kind=market_awareness: their answer is a dated snapshot bound to live data at drill time, not a stored fact.

items.q: What is a bond?
items.a:
A securitised loan: the issuer raises principal today, pays coupons over the life and repays at 100 at
maturity. The components are nominal, coupon and payment frequency, tenor or maturity, rank in the capital
structure, and anything optional - call rights, step-ups, change-of-control put.
rubric: Names nominal, coupon and frequency, tenor, rank, and optionality
Says the issuer raises principal today and repays at 100 at maturity
Names tradability as what separates a bond from a loan
mistakes: Describing a bond as 'a loan' with no mention of the transferable claim.

items.q: Why do bond prices fall when rates rise?
items.a:
Because the coupon is fixed. If the market pays 4% today for the same risk and my bond has a 3% coupon,
nobody buys it at 100. The price has to fall until the yield to maturity matches 4% again. Mathematically: the
price is the present value of fixed payments - if the discount rate rises, the present value falls.
rubric: States that the coupon is fixed while the market rate moves
Says the price falls until the yield to maturity matches the market rate
Reaches for the present-value framing unprompted
mistakes: Giving only the intuition and never naming discounting.

items.q: How do you price a bond?
items.a:
Present value of all cash flows: P = Σ C/(1+y)^t + N/(1+y)^T. Cleaner would be to discount
each cash flow at the matching zero rate off the curve rather than at a single YTM - the YTM is a simplification
that assumes the curve is flat and that you can reinvest all coupons at y.

Worked example if he wants one: 5 years, 3% annual coupon, market yield 4%. Price ≈ 3 × annuity
factor(4%, 5y) + 100/(1.04)^5 = 3 × 4.4518 + 82.19 ≈ 95.55. So a discount bond, because coupon < yield.
rubric: Gives the present value formula: sum of coupons plus principal, discounted
Notes that discounting each cash flow at the matching zero rate is cleaner than one YTM
States the YTM assumes a flat curve and reinvestment at y
mistakes: Saying 'I would have to calculate that' instead of using the annuity shortcut.

items.q: Clean vs dirty price?
items.a:
The clean price is the quoted price excluding accrued interest; the dirty price is what actually gets
paid - clean plus interest accrued since the last coupon date. You quote clean because otherwise the dirty price
sawtooths upward between coupon dates and drops on the coupon date, which would make price comparisons useless.
rubric: Clean price excludes accrued interest, dirty price is what is actually paid
Explains why: the dirty price sawtooths between coupon dates, ruining comparison
Knows the EUR corporate convention is ACT/ACT (ICMA), annual
mistakes: Giving the definitions without the 'why quote clean'.

items.q: Coupon vs current yield vs YTM?
items.a:
The coupon is the fixed payment on the nominal. Current yield is coupon divided by current price - it
ignores capital gain or loss to maturity. The YTM is the internal rate of return of all cash flows, so it's the
only one of the three that combines coupon, time and price movement.

Ordering for a discount bond: coupon < current yield < YTM. For a premium bond, exactly the reverse.
rubric: Coupon is fixed on nominal; current yield is coupon over price; YTM is the IRR of all cash flows
Says only the YTM combines coupon, time and price movement
Gives the ordering: for a discount bond coupon < current yield < YTM, reversed for a premium bond
mistakes: Getting the ordering backwards. Derive it: a discount bond has a capital gain to come, so YTM is highest.

items.q: What are the flaws of YTM?
items.a:
Two assumptions: it assumes all coupons are reinvested at the YTM, and that the bond is held to
maturity. Neither is usually true - reinvestment risk is real, and for a callable bond the relevant measure is
yield-to-call or yield-to-worst.
rubric: Names the reinvestment-at-YTM assumption
Names the hold-to-maturity assumption
Names yield-to-worst as the measure actually quoted for callable paper
mistakes: Listing the assumptions without naming yield-to-worst.

items.q: Duration: Macaulay vs modified?
items.a:
Macaulay duration is the average, present-value-weighted time to receipt of cash flows, in years.
Modified duration is Macaulay divided by (1+y) and measures price sensitivity: ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod × Δy.
In practice 'duration' almost always means modified duration.

Example: D_mod = 7, yield rises 50bp → price falls roughly 3.5%.
rubric: Macaulay is the PV-weighted average time to receipt, in years
Modified is Macaulay divided by (1+y) and measures price sensitivity
Gives the relation dP/P is approximately minus modified duration times dy, with a worked number
mistakes: Knowing the formula but having no worked number ready.

items.q: What drives duration?
items.a:
Three drivers. Longer maturity → higher duration. Lower coupon → higher duration, because more present
value sits at the end. Lower yield → higher duration, because late cash flows are discounted less heavily. The
extreme case is the zero coupon bond: there Macaulay duration equals the remaining maturity exactly.
rubric: Longer maturity raises duration
Lower coupon raises duration, because more present value sits at the end
Lower yield raises duration
Uses the zero-coupon case, where Macaulay duration equals maturity, as the proof
mistakes: Reciting three rules with no mechanism behind them.

items.q: What is DV01?
items.a:
The price change in currency terms for a one basis point move in yield.
DV01 ≈ D_mod × price × 0.0001. Duration is the percentage view, DV01 the absolute one - on a trading
desk you work with DV01 because you hedge positions in euros per basis point, not in percent.
rubric: Defines DV01 as the currency price change for a one basis point yield move
Gives DV01 as approximately modified duration times price times 0.0001
Explains why a desk uses it: hedging is in euros per basis point, not percent
mistakes: Conflating DV01 with duration rather than naming it as the absolute view.

items.q: What is convexity and why is it valuable?
items.a:
Convexity is the second derivative of price with respect to yield - the curvature of the price-yield
relationship. Duration alone is a straight line and understates the price in both directions.
It's valuable because it works asymmetrically: when yields fall the price rises more than duration predicts,
and when yields rise it falls less. So positive convexity is a free advantage - and that's why the investor pays
for it in the form of a slightly lower yield. For callable bonds convexity can turn negative, because the call
caps the price upside.
rubric: Defines convexity as the curvature of the price-yield relationship, the second derivative
States the asymmetry: prices rise more than duration predicts and fall less
Says positive convexity is paid for through a slightly lower yield
Notes convexity turns negative for callable bonds because the call caps upside
mistakes: Missing the negative convexity on callables, which is what separates an intermediate answer.

items.q: What types of bonds are there?
items.a:
By coupon: fixed, floaters against Euribor, zero coupon, inflation-linked. By optionality: callable,
puttable, convertible. By rank: senior unsecured, senior secured, subordinated, and corporate hybrids as a
perpetual subordinated structure. By format: benchmark bond, private placement, Schuldschein - though strictly
speaking that isn't a bond at all, it's a loan.
rubric: Classifies by coupon (fixed, floater, zero, linker)
Classifies by optionality (callable, puttable, convertible)
Classifies by rank (senior unsecured, secured, subordinated, hybrid)
Notes the Schuldschein is not strictly a bond at all
mistakes: A flat list with no organising axis.

items.q: How does a floating rate note work?
items.a:
The coupon resets periodically, typically 3M or 6M Euribor plus a fixed margin. That makes the
interest rate duration very short - it only runs to the next fixing - but the spread duration runs over the full
life. Which means: a floater protects against interest rate moves, not against spread widening.

The relevant yield measure is the discount margin, not the YTM.
rubric: Coupon resets against 3M or 6M Euribor plus a fixed margin
Interest rate duration is short, running only to the next fixing
Spread duration runs over the full life, so a floater does not protect against spread widening
Names the discount margin as the relevant yield measure
mistakes: Saying a floater 'has no duration'. It has no rate duration; it has full spread duration.

items.q: What does the yield curve tell you?
items.a:
It shows yields across maturities. Normally upward sloping means the market demands a premium for
committing longer and expects no rate cuts. Flat means uncertainty about the path. Inverted usually means the
market is pricing rate cuts - historically often a recession signal.
For the issuer the steepness is directly relevant: a steep curve makes short maturities cheap and pushes
issuance to the front end; a flat curve makes it almost free to issue long.
rubric: Reads upward-sloping, flat and inverted correctly
Names the inversion as pricing rate cuts and historically a recession signal
Lands on the issuer implication: a steep curve pushes issuance to the front end
mistakes: A macro-class answer that never reaches the issuance decision.

items.q: What exactly is the mid-swap rate?
items.a:
The midpoint of bid and offer for the fixed leg of an interest rate swap of the corresponding
maturity - in the EUR market conventionally against 6M Euribor. It's the reference point because it represents a
tenor-matched, liquid and largely credit-risk-free rate against which spreads can be compared cleanly.
rubric: Defines it as the mid of bid and offer on the fixed leg of a matched-maturity swap
Notes the EUR convention is against 6M Euribor
Explains why it is the reference: tenor-matched, liquid and largely credit-risk-free
mistakes: Confusing the mid-swap reference for bond pricing with the OIS/ESTR discounting curve.

items.q: Why price over mid-swaps rather than Bunds?
items.a:
Three reasons. First, the swap curve is continuously available for every maturity, whereas there are
only a limited number of Bund benchmarks. Second, the Bund is no longer a neutral reference point - it trades with
its own scarcity premium, or depending on the market phase with a concession because of issuance volume. And third,
most institutional investors hedge and fund against Euribor, not against Bunds - so the swap is closer to their
actual funding.
That's why a pricing update usually shows both: the level against swaps and against Bunds, because the swap
spread itself moves.
rubric: Swap curve is continuously available at every maturity; Bund benchmarks are few
Bund is not neutral: it carries its own scarcity premium or supply concession
Investors hedge and fund against Euribor, not against Bunds
Notes a pricing update shows both, because the swap spread itself moves
mistakes: Giving only the availability argument and missing that the Bund is not a neutral reference.

items.q: How is the coupon of a new issue fixed?
items.a:
At pricing the spread is fixed first. The yield then follows from the mid-swap rate for that maturity
at the moment of fixing, plus the final spread. The coupon is then rounded - usually to an eighth or a quarter of a
percent - so that the bond is issued at or just below 100.
rubric: The spread is fixed first at pricing
The yield follows from the mid-swap rate at the moment of fixing plus the final spread
The coupon is a rounded output, set so the bond prices at or just below par
mistakes: Treating the coupon as the input. It is the output, and it is rounded.

items.q: Why buy 10y over 5y?
items.a:
Because of the term premium and the duration. With an upward-sloping curve he gets more yield for
waiting, and if he's positioning for falling rates the higher duration gives him more leverage. On top of that
there's a structural reason for insurers and pension funds: they have to duration-match long-dated liabilities,
and there simply isn't suitable material at the short end.
rubric: Names the term premium on an upward-sloping curve
Names higher duration as leverage on a view that rates fall
Names the structural bid: insurers and pension funds duration-matching long liabilities
mistakes: Giving only the yield-pickup answer and missing liability matching.

items.q: What makes up the yield of a corporate bond?
items.a:
From the bottom up: the risk-free or reference rate for the tenor - in the EUR market the mid-swap
rate. On top of that the credit spread, which compensates for probability of default and expected loss given
default. Embedded in that is effectively a liquidity premium too - a small, rarely traded bond yields more than a
liquid benchmark of the same issuer. And finally, where applicable, an option premium for call rights.
For a new issue, the new issue premium comes on top of all that.
rubric: Reference rate for the tenor, in EUR the mid-swap rate
Credit spread for probability of default and loss given default
Liquidity premium as a separate layer
Option premium where there are call rights, plus the new issue premium on top for a new deal
mistakes: Giving two layers and stopping. Naming liquidity separately is what lets you argue a new benchmark prices inside a stale line.

items.q: Spread measures compared?
items.a:
G-spread: yield minus the yield of the nearest-maturity government bond. Crude, because the
maturities rarely match exactly.
I-spread: yield minus the interpolated swap rate of the same maturity. Simple and widely used in practice.
Z-spread: the constant add-on to the entire zero swap curve at which the present value of all cash flows
equals the market price. Cleaner than the I-spread because it accounts for the shape of the curve rather than just
one point.
ASW (asset swap spread): the spread over Euribor an investor earns by buying the fixed-coupon bond and
swapping the fixed rate into floating. That's the standard measure for secondary comparison.
OAS: z-spread adjusted for the value of embedded options - relevant for callable bonds and hybrids.
rubric: G-spread is against the nearest government bond and is crude on maturity mismatch
I-spread is against the interpolated swap rate at the same maturity
Z-spread is the constant add-on to the whole zero curve that reprices the bond
ASW is the spread over Euribor from buying fixed and swapping to floating; OAS is z-spread adjusted for options
mistakes: Treating z-spread and ASW as interchangeable. They converge near par and diverge away from it.

items.q: Walk me through pricing a new issue.
items.a:
Six steps, about a minute in total:
1. Build the issuer's own curve. Take the outstanding bonds, pull ASW or z-spread levels, plot them by
maturity. What matters is that the levels are tradeable and not merely quoted.
2. Interpolate to the target tenor. Usually the issuer has no bond at exactly that point. So interpolate
between the two nearest points and account for the steepness of the credit curve.
3. Build a comparables set. Same rating band, same sector, similar leverage and tenor. The peers matter
more the thinner, more illiquid or more stale the issuer's own curve is. Also look at where the peers priced their
most recent new issues and how those traded afterwards.
4. Derive fair value. The interpolated level, adjusted for liquidity - a large new benchmark should trade
tighter than a small old line - and for anything that has changed in the credit since those bonds last traded.
5. Add the new issue premium. The concession over fair value that gets investors to participate.
6. Set IPTs above the target and tighten through guidance steps until book size and price line up."
rubric: Builds the issuer's own curve first from outstanding bonds on ASW or z-spread
Interpolates to the target tenor and allows for credit curve steepness
Builds a comparable set second, weighted more heavily the thinner the issuer's own curve
Derives fair value adjusted for liquidity, then adds the new issue premium, then sets IPTs above and tightens
mistakes: Starting with comps. That is what you do when there is no issuer curve, which is the exception.

items.q: How do you select a peer group?
items.a:
Primarily three axes: rating or credit quality, sector and tenor. Then secondarily:
size and leverage, currency and format of issuance, and how current the levels are - a bond that hasn't traded in
three weeks is worth little as a reference.
And I'd always filter on issuance date: a bond issued two years ago in a completely different rate environment,
trading well below par today, has a different buyer profile than a new issue at par. That distorts the
comparison.
rubric: Primary axes: rating or credit quality, sector, tenor
Secondary: size and leverage, currency and format, and how current the levels are
Filters on issuance date, because a low-coupon legacy bond at a deep discount has a different buyer profile
mistakes: Omitting issuance date. Legacy discount paper attracts technical buyers and its spread is not a clean read.

items.q: Thin peer group with high beta - what then?
items.a:
Then I'd separate two things: the level and the sensitivity.
On the level I'd widen the net - either the same sector abroad, or the same rating in an adjacent sector
with a similar cash flow profile. The important thing is to make that step deliberately and to say so openly,
rather than pretending I have a clean comparable set.
On the beta: if the few peers have a high beta, that means their spreads move disproportionately to the
overall market. Then the current point value tells you less than the question of where we are in the market cycle.
In a tight market, high-beta names look artificially good; so I'd look at an average over a longer window, or at
the ratio to the index, rather than at yesterday's close.
And in practice that would change the case too: a high beta increases the uncertainty around fair value, and
you pay for uncertainty with a higher new issue premium.
rubric: Separates the level question from the sensitivity question
Widens the net deliberately and says so, rather than pretending the comp set is clean
Says a high beta means the current point value matters less than where the market cycle is
Connects uncertainty in fair value to a higher new issue premium
mistakes: Not making the last link: uncertainty is paid for in the NIP, which turns pricing into a risk decision rather than arithmetic.

items.q: What is the new issue premium and where is it now?
items.a:
Definition: "The concession the issuer pays over the fair value of its own secondary curve to get
investors into the new issue. Economically it compensates the investor for absorbing new paper, taking on duration
and bearing the risk that the bond trades worse - plus simply the incentive to write an order at all."
Measurement: "Ex post you calculate it as the final reoffer spread minus fair value on the same curve at
the moment of pricing."
Currently: "In the first half of the year concessions in EUR IG were very tight - in places low single
digits. But in July they rose to the highest level of the year, because the Middle East situation and rate
volatility have made investors more price sensitive and the books have thinned out."
rubric: Defines it as the concession over fair value on the issuer's own secondary curve
Explains what it compensates: absorbing new paper, duration, trading risk, and the incentive to order at all
Measures it ex post as final reoffer spread minus fair value at the moment of pricing
Can say where it currently sits and in which direction it has moved
mistakes: Quoting a stale level. NIPs move; check before quoting one.

items.q: Why should a new benchmark price inside an existing line?
items.a:
Because of the liquidity premium. A new benchmark of €500m or more is index-eligible, actively quoted
by sales and tradeable. An old line of €300m, half of which sits in buy-and-hold portfolios, barely trades - and
the investor demands compensation for that.
Which means: fair value isn't simply the observed secondary spread, it's the secondary spread corrected for that
liquidity difference. In practice that pulls fair value somewhat tighter relative to an illiquid legacy bond.
rubric: Names the liquidity premium as the reason
A new benchmark is index-eligible, quoted and tradeable; an old small line barely trades
Concludes fair value is the observed secondary spread corrected for the liquidity difference
mistakes: Treating the observed secondary spread as fair value without the liquidity correction. This is the most common way a naive fair value goes wrong.

items.q: How do you set IPTs?
items.a:
You set IPTs deliberately generously relative to the expected landing point - in EUR IG typically with
around 20 to 35 basis points of tightening room, depending on volatility and how well known the name is. The
purpose is to build a broad, honest book before you tighten.
The calculus is asymmetric: start too generous and you lose a few basis points of negotiating position, but you
can still tighten. Start too tight and the book doesn't come together - and a deal that doesn't cover or has to be
pulled costs the issuer far more than a few basis points, because he comes back more expensively next time.
rubric: IPTs are set deliberately generously relative to the expected landing point
Gives the tightening room as a conditional range, wider when volatility is high
Gives the asymmetry: too generous costs basis points, too tight risks a deal that does not cover
mistakes: Presenting the range as a fixed rule rather than conditional on volatility and how well known the name is.

items.q: How do you tighten, and how do you know when you've gone too far?
items.a:
You tighten in steps and watch two things: how much book is lost at each step, and who leaves. A book
that shrinks from 3.5x to 2.8x is normal. One that halves, or where the large real money orders drop out, tells me
the last step went too far.
The second piece of information is the price limits: if a large share of orders has a limit exactly at the
current level, the next tightening is expensive.
And the real test only comes afterwards - how the bond trades the next day. If it trades meaningfully wider than
reoffer, the last step was too aggressive, regardless of how the book looked.
rubric: Watches how much book is lost at each step and, more importantly, who leaves
Distinguishes losing fast money (fine) from losing large real money orders (a warning)
Reads the price limits: a book full of limits at the current level makes the next step expensive
Names next-day secondary performance as the real test
mistakes: Watching only the coverage ratio. Who leaves matters more than how much.

items.q: What drives credit spreads?
items.a:
I'd separate it into four blocks. Macro and risk appetite - in a risk-off move spreads widen
because investors rotate into government bonds. Fundamentals - leverage, earnings, rating actions,
sector-specific shocks like energy prices. Technicals - primary market supply, fund flows into credit, and
who has dropped out as a buyer. Rate volatility - that's a driver in its own right, because high rate
volatility makes investors more price sensitive generally, independent of the credit.
Right now the last one is the most relevant: spreads are tight, but rate volatility is high, and that's exactly
why new issue premiums are rising even though secondary spreads haven't widened.
rubric: Macro and risk appetite
Fundamentals: leverage, earnings, rating actions, sector shocks
Technicals: primary supply, fund flows, who has stopped buying
Rate volatility as a driver in its own right, independent of the credit
mistakes: Missing rate volatility as a separate driver. It is why NIPs can rise while secondary spreads stay tight.

items.q: Rate duration vs spread duration?
items.a:
Rate duration measures the price response to a shift in the risk-free curve; spread duration the
response to a change in the credit spread. For a fixed-coupon bond the two are numerically almost identical. For a
floater they diverge: rate duration is effectively zero until the next fixing, spread duration runs over the full
life.
Practically that means: an investor who wants to avoid rate risk but keep credit risk buys a floater - or asset
swaps a fixed-coupon bond.
rubric: Rate duration is sensitivity to the risk-free curve; spread duration to the credit spread
Notes they are numerically almost identical for a fixed-coupon bullet
Notes they diverge for a floater: rate duration near zero, spread duration full life
Draws the practical conclusion: buy a floater or asset swap to keep credit and drop rate risk
mistakes: Assuming the two are always the same because they usually are.

items.q: What is the swap spread and why does it move?
items.a:
The difference between the swap rate and the yield of the matched-maturity Bund. It moves because each
leg has its own drivers: the Bund responds to supply and to safe-haven demand, the swap to bank credit risk and to
hedging flows.
It matters for us because an issuer who prices over mid-swaps but evaluates the outcome in Bund terms feels a
shift in the swap spread directly. That's why a pricing update usually shows both levels.
Right now the driver is mainly German issuance volume - Germany is funding infrastructure and defence through
record issuance while the ECB no longer reinvests. More Bund supply with fewer price-insensitive buyers pushes the
Bund price down, lifts its yield, and thereby compresses the swap spread.
rubric: Defines it as swap rate minus matched-maturity Bund yield
Names the separate drivers on each leg: Bund supply and safe-haven demand versus bank credit and hedging flows
Explains why it matters: an issuer pricing over swaps but judging in Bund terms feels the move directly
mistakes: Getting the sign wrong on the supply mechanics. If unsure, give the definition and the drivers and stop.

items.q: No comparables at the target tenor - what do you do?
items.a:
Interpolate and justify the premium. I'd take the 10-year and 15-year points of the issuer's own curve,
interpolate to 12 years and allow for the fact that credit curves usually flatten between 10 and 15 years. Then I'd
sanity-check against peers who have actually issued at the long end, to see how much the market has recently
demanded for the extra years.
And I'd play the question back: if there is no liquid market there, the honest answer may be that 12 years is
the wrong format - and that a Schuldschein or a private placement delivers that tenor more cheaply than a benchmark
bond for which you'd first have to create the market.
rubric: Interpolates between the surrounding points on the issuer's own curve
Allows for credit curves flattening at the long end
Sanity-checks against peers who have actually printed at that tenor
Plays the question back: if there is no market at that tenor, a Schuldschein or private placement may be the right product
mistakes: Guessing harder instead of asking whether the format is wrong.

items.q: What is a greenium?
items.a:
The - usually small - pricing advantage an issuer gets on a green bond relative to a comparable
conventional bond on the same curve, often in the range of a few basis points. It comes from demand: there are
mandated ESG funds that have to buy green paper, while supply is limited.
Honestly, the effect is contested and varies a lot - in tight markets it shrinks to essentially nothing, because
then everything is oversubscribed anyway. The more robust benefit is usually not the spread but the diversification
of the investor base and a better-supported book in difficult market phases.
rubric: Defines it as the pricing advantage of a green bond over a comparable conventional bond
Explains the source: mandated ESG demand against limited supply
Is appropriately sceptical: the effect is contested, small, and shrinks in tight markets
Names the more robust benefit as investor base diversification and book resilience
mistakes: Either dismissing the greenium entirely or overclaiming it. Both read as unfamiliarity.

items.q: Origination vs syndicate?
items.a:
Origination is the issuer side: the relationship with the treasurer and CFO, capital structure and
funding advice, pitches, rating advisory, preparing documentation. Syndicate is the investor side and the market
side: where is the window, what is fair value, what does demand look like, how do we execute, how do we allocate.
Put differently: origination brings the transaction to the table, syndicate takes it through the market. And
because syndicate speaks to investors daily, it has the more current information on price levels - which is why the
price recommendation comes from syndicate, even though the relationship sits with origination.
rubric: Origination is the issuer side: relationship, capital structure and funding advice, pitching
Syndicate is the investor and market side: window, fair value, execution, allocation
Explains the reason for the split: syndicate talks to investors daily, so the price recommendation sits there
mistakes: Describing the org chart without the reason for the split. Also: do not caricature origination.

items.q: Who else is involved in a deal?
items.a:
On our side: origination as the client interface, syndicate for price and execution, DCM sales for
the investor dialogue, the trading desk for secondary market and market making after pricing, legal and
documentation for the prospectus or programme, compliance for insider lists and wall crossing, and
depending on the case rating advisory and corporate treasury solutions for hedging.
On the other side: the issuer - usually treasury - its lawyers, the rating agencies, the paying agent and the
exchange for the listing.
rubric: Names origination, syndicate, DCM sales, and the trading desk as separate functions
Names legal/documentation and compliance
Names the issuer side: treasury, its counsel, rating agencies, paying agent, exchange
mistakes: Saying syndicate 'manages secondary trading'. It does not. The trading desk makes the market; syndicate monitors performance.

items.q: Walk me through the deal timeline.
items.a:
Roughly four phases:
Preparation, weeks to months ahead: mandating, documentation - either a drawdown under the EMTN programme
or a standalone issue - the rating process if needed, and ongoing market monitoring with pricing updates.
Pre-marketing, days ahead: depending on how well known the name is, investor calls or a short roadshow,
sometimes pre-sounding under wall crossing.
Execution day: announcement in the morning, usually around 8:30-9:00 CET; IPTs out, books open; the book
builds through the morning; guidance with a first tightening, often together with a size indication; 'books
subject'; then launch with final size and final spread; pricing in the afternoon with the coupon fixed against the
mid-swap rate.
After pricing: allocation, free to trade, settlement usually T+5 in the EUR market, listing, and
monitoring of secondary performance.
rubric: Preparation: mandate, documentation (EMTN drawdown or standalone), rating, pricing updates
Pre-marketing: investor calls or a short roadshow, sometimes pre-sounding under wall crossing
Execution day: announcement with IPTs in the morning, guidance, books subject, launch, pricing in the afternoon
After pricing: allocation, free to trade, settlement, listing, secondary monitoring
mistakes: Describing a multi-week process. Most EUR benchmark deals are same-day intraday executions.

items.q: What are the syndicate roles on a deal?
items.a:
Global coordinator - coordinates structure, process and documentation, usually the bank with the
closest relationship. Active bookrunner - actively runs the book, speaks to investors, makes the price
recommendation, holds allocation authority together with the issuer. Passive bookrunner - appears on the
ticket and in the league table but isn't operationally involved in price leadership. Co-lead or co-manager - 
a small role, often mandated for relationship reasons, for instance because the bank is a lender.
For execution what matters most is how many active bookrunners there are - too many make price discovery
sluggish, because more houses have to agree.
rubric: Global coordinator coordinates structure, process and documentation
Active bookrunner runs the book, makes the price recommendation, holds allocation authority
Passive bookrunner appears on the ticket and in the league table but does not lead price
Notes too many actives slow price discovery
mistakes: Not knowing the active versus passive distinction, which is genuinely load-bearing.

items.q: Why mandate several banks?
items.a:
Three reasons. Distribution - different houses have different investor relationships, more banks
means a broader book. Relationship economics - the banks that provide the issuer's credit lines expect fee
business in return; a mandate is that consideration. And insurance - several opinions on price and on the
window reduce the risk of getting it wrong.
The price of that is coordination effort and shared fees.
rubric: Distribution: different houses reach different investors
Relationship economics: lending banks are rewarded with fee business
Insurance: several opinions on price and window reduce the risk of getting it wrong
Names the cost: coordination effort and shared fees
mistakes: Missing relationship economics, which is how the market actually works.

items.q: Pot deal vs retention?
items.a:
In a pot deal all orders go into a common book that all bookrunners can see; allocation is
decided by the issuer together with the leads, and investor names are transparent. That's the standard in the
European IG market.
Under retention, each bank receives a fixed allotment to place itself. That's more common for retail
tranches or in certain local markets.
The advantage of the pot process is transparency: the issuer sees who is really buying and can deliberately
favour real money.
rubric: Pot deal: one common book visible to all bookrunners, allocation decided by issuer with the leads
Retention: each bank gets a fixed allotment to place itself
Names the pot as European IG standard and transparency as its advantage
mistakes: Not knowing which is standard in European IG.

items.q: How does the bank make money on a bond deal?
items.a:
Through the issuance fee, which is retained from the proceeds - for European IG corporates typically in
the order of roughly 15 to 35 basis points of the volume, depending on tenor, format and credit quality; materially
more for hybrids and high yield. The fee is split among the banks by role, with active bookrunners taking the
largest share.
On top of that, indirectly: secondary trading, hedging business, and the league table credit, which in turn
attracts mandates.
rubric: Names the issuance fee retained from proceeds and gives it as a range, flagged as a range
Notes the fee is split by role with active bookrunners taking the largest share
Names the indirect economics: secondary trading, hedging, and league table credit driving future mandates
mistakes: Quoting a precise fee figure. These vary and are not public; a confident wrong number is worse than a range.

items.q: What's in the announcement?
items.a:
Issuer, rating, format and rank, tenor or maturity, expected size - often just 'benchmark' - the bank
group with roles, and the IPTs. Plus references to selling restrictions, so Reg S, and whether it's a green or
sustainability-linked format.
After that the books open, sales approaches investors, and we watch how fast and with what quality the orders
come in. The first ninety minutes often already tell you whether the deal is going well.
rubric: Names issuer, rating, format and rank, tenor, expected size, bank group with roles, and IPTs
Notes selling restrictions and any green or sustainability-linked format
Says 'benchmark' is often used instead of a size, preserving the issuer's optionality
mistakes: Committing to a size in the announcement when the book has not told you what is achievable.

items.q: How do you read an orderbook?
items.a:
Six things, and size is not the most important one:
Coverage ratio - book size divided by deal size. Three to four times is healthy on a benchmark. Ten times
usually means it was launched too cheap.
Granularity - many mid-sized orders are more robust than three large ones. Concentration means one
investor can dictate the outcome or dump the paper later.
Price sensitivity - how many orders have a limit and where it sits. A book that looks large but is full of
limits at IPT level isn't really large.
Investor quality - real money versus fast money. Asset managers, insurers and pension funds hold; hedge
funds and some bank books flip on day one.
Attrition - the difference between peak book and final book. Heavy attrition on tightening means the last
step went too far.
Anchor orders - a large early commitment gives the deal credibility and lets the rest of the book build
around it.
rubric: Opens by saying size is not the most important thing
Coverage ratio, with a sense of what is healthy and what signals it was launched too cheap
Granularity, price sensitivity and where limits sit
Investor quality (real money versus fast money), attrition, and anchor orders
mistakes: Reading only the coverage ratio. A book full of limits at IPT level is not really large.

items.q: What does 'books subject' mean?
items.a:
That's the announcement that the books are only open subject to further price revision - in practice
the last opportunity for investors to confirm or withdraw their order before the final spread is set. It forces the
book to be honest: whoever isn't there at that level drops out now rather than at allocation.
rubric: Defines it as books open only subject to further price revision
Notes it is the last chance for investors to confirm or withdraw before the final spread
Explains the function: it forces the book to be honest before allocation
mistakes: Not being able to define it at all. It comes up naturally in any bookbuild description.

items.q: How do you allocate?
items.a:
Not pro rata, but on quality. Preference goes to investors who ordered early and without a limit, who
hold the name long term, who are also there in difficult market phases, and who are strategically important to the
issuer - for instance because he needs them as an anchor in future transactions.
Disadvantaged are orders that are clearly aiming to flip, and inflated orders speculating on a scaleback.
Formally the issuer decides, in practice on syndicate's recommendation - because we know who behaved how. That
is exactly what the desk maintains the investor database for.
rubric: Allocation is on quality, not pro rata
Favours early, unlimited orders, long-term holders, and strategically important accounts
Penalises likely flippers and inflated orders speculating on a scaleback
Notes the issuer formally decides on syndicate's recommendation, informed by the investor database
mistakes: Saying allocation is pro rata. It is a judgement about behaviour.

items.q: What's a good break performance?
items.a:
A few basis points tighter than reoffer. Enough that investors are rewarded and order again next time
 - but not so much that the issuer visibly left money on the table.
If the bond trades meaningfully wider, the pricing was too aggressive and the issuer pays for it next time. If it
trades ten basis points tighter, the concession was too generous. Both are mistakes, just with different victims.
rubric: A few basis points tighter than reoffer
Explains why: investors are rewarded and order again, without the issuer visibly leaving money behind
Names both failure modes: trading wider means pricing was too aggressive, ten tighter means the concession was too generous
mistakes: Treating a big tightening on the break as an unambiguous success. It means the issuer overpaid.

items.q: The deal breaks wide - what now?
items.a:
First, understand whether it's the deal or the market. If the whole index widened that day, it isn't a
pricing error. If only our bond trades worse, it is.
Then look for the cause in the book: was it concentration, was there too much fast money, was the tightening too
far too late. That insight goes into the investor database and into the next allocation.
And be honest with the issuer. A treasurer who gets a straight assessment after a poor issue mandates again. One
who gets it sugar-coated doesn't.
rubric: First separates a market move from a deal-specific move by checking the index
Looks for the cause in the book: concentration, too much fast money, tightening too far too late
Feeds the finding into the investor database and the next allocation
Is honest with the issuer
mistakes: Saying 'we stabilise'. There is no formal price stabilisation in corporate bond syndication the way there is in ECM.

items.q: What is pre-sounding / wall crossing?
items.a:
A confidential advance contact with a small number of selected investors, to test appetite for a
format or a size before announcing publicly. The investors involved are brought over the wall - they receive inside
information, are placed on an insider list, and are restricted from trading the name until announcement.
That's regulatorily sensitive, runs through compliance, and is therefore used sparingly - typically for difficult
structures like hybrids, for debut issuers, or for unusually large volumes.
rubric: Confidential advance contact with a small number of selected investors to test appetite
The investors receive inside information, go on an insider list, and are restricted from trading
Notes it runs through compliance and is used sparingly: hybrids, debut issuers, unusually large size
mistakes: Describing it as a marketing call. The trading restriction is the cost and the whole compliance point.

items.q: What makes a good issuance window?
items.a:
Four conditions: the issuer isn't in a blackout period, i.e. after results; there's no major data
release or central bank meeting that day; rate volatility is manageable; and the market isn't overloaded with
supply in the same sector.
In practice that means: Tuesday to Thursday, European morning, not on the day of US CPI or an ECB meeting, and
ideally in a week where three comparable names aren't bringing the same format.
And seasonally: January and September are the densest months, August is effectively dead, and from late November
the market shuts.
rubric: Issuer not in blackout after results
No major data release or central bank meeting that day
Manageable rate volatility and no supply pile-up in the same sector
Names the seasonality: January and September densest, August dead, market shuts from late November
mistakes: Naming only 'good market conditions' with no specific conditions behind it.

items.q: Why do a dual- or triple-tranche deal?
items.a:
To serve different investor bases in one go and to smooth the maturity profile. At the short end bank
books and money-market-adjacent investors buy, at the long end insurers and pension funds. Anyone trying to place
€1.5bn in a single maturity has to stretch the market a long way; spread across three maturities the same amount is
easier and often cheaper to place overall.
The downside is execution complexity: you run three books in parallel and have to balance between tranches when
one goes better than another.
rubric: Serves different investor bases in one go: short end to bank books, long end to insurers
Smooths the maturity profile
Explains why it is often cheaper than stretching one maturity for the full size
Names the cost: parallel books and balancing between tranches
mistakes: Missing that this is the same logic as Schuldschein tranching.

items.q: What is liability management?
items.a:
Active management of existing liabilities rather than only issuing new debt. The three usual tools:
tender offer - buying back outstanding bonds for cash, usually alongside a new issue, to extend the maturity
profile. Exchange offer - swapping old bonds into new ones. And make-whole call - early redemption at
a price that compensates the investor for the forgone cash flows, discounted at a narrow spread over the government
yield.
The typical trigger is an approaching maturity wall or a coupon that no longer fits the new rate environment.
rubric: Names tender offer: buying back outstanding bonds for cash, usually alongside a new issue
Names exchange offer: swapping old bonds into new ones
Names make-whole call and defines the discount rate as government yield plus a narrow spread
Names the trigger: a maturity wall or a coupon that no longer fits the rate environment
mistakes: Defining make-whole without the discount rate, which is what makes early calls expensive and why par call periods exist.

items.q: EMTN programme vs standalone?
items.a:
An EMTN programme is framework documentation under which an issuer can draw repeatedly and very
quickly - the base prospectus is in place, all you need are final terms. That reduces time and cost per transaction
substantially and enables opportunistic issuance, including in small sizes via reverse enquiry.
A standalone issue is documented for a single transaction. That makes sense for infrequent issuers for whom the
annual update of a programme doesn't pay off.
rubric: EMTN is framework documentation: base prospectus in place, only final terms needed per drawdown
Explains the benefit: speed and cost per transaction, enabling opportunistic and small issuance
Standalone is documented for a single transaction, suiting infrequent issuers
mistakes: Missing the speed point, which is why programmes exist: decision to announcement in hours.

items.q: Reg S vs 144A?
items.a:
Both are exemptions from US securities law. Reg S means: distribution exclusively outside the
US, no SEC registration, and correspondingly lower disclosure and liability requirements. 144A additionally
permits distribution to qualified institutional buyers in the US, but requires substantially more disclosure, often
US GAAP reconciliations, and brings US liability risk with it.
A typical European IG corporate issues Reg S only, because US demand doesn't justify the extra work. But as soon
as you need size in USD or a broad US investor base, 144A/Reg S becomes the format - and for emerging-markets
issuers in EUR, Reg S only is the norm.
rubric: Both are exemptions from US registration
Reg S: distribution outside the US only, lower disclosure and liability
144A: adds distribution to QIBs in the US, with more disclosure and US liability risk
Notes a typical European IG corporate issues Reg S only
mistakes: Describing 144A as 'a US listing'. It is a private resale exemption, not registration.

items.q: How would you build a pricing update?
items.a:
Top down. First, market context: where are mid-swaps across the relevant maturities, where is
the 10-year Bund, how has the credit index - say iTraxx Main - moved since the last update, what was the week's
primary volume.
Second, the issuer's own curve: all outstanding bonds with maturity, coupon, size, ASW and z-spread levels,
and the change from the prior week.
Third, the comparables set: the same fields for the peers, grouped by rating, plus their most recent new
issues with reoffer spread and current level, so you can see how those traded.
Fourth, the derivation: interpolated fair value for the relevant target tenors and an indicative range for
a new issue spread.
And formally important: identical layout in every edition, so changes jump out - and every number with a source
and a timestamp.
rubric: Market context first: mid-swaps across maturities, the 10y Bund, the credit index, weekly primary volume
The issuer's own curve: every outstanding bond with maturity, coupon, size, ASW and z-spread, and the weekly change
The comparable set with the same fields, plus peers' recent new issues and how they traded
Derivation: interpolated fair value and an indicative new issue range
Identical layout every edition, every number with a source and a timestamp
mistakes: Producing a different layout each week. Changes are supposed to jump out.

items.q: What would you analyse in an orderbook review?
items.a:
Five cuts: by investor type - asset managers, insurers and pension funds, banks, hedge funds,
central banks; by geography; by order size, to make concentration visible; by price sensitivity,
i.e. the share of limited orders and where the limits sat; and attrition across the guidance steps, i.e. who
dropped out at which level.
And then the comparison: the same metrics for comparable transactions in the same sector and rating over recent
months. A book in isolation says little - it becomes interesting in comparison.
rubric: Cuts by investor type, geography, order size, and price sensitivity
Analyses attrition across the guidance steps: who dropped out at which level
Compares against similar transactions in the same sector and rating
mistakes: Presenting the book in isolation. It only becomes an analysis in comparison.

items.q: What is reverse enquiry?
items.a:
The reverse route: rather than the bank proposing a transaction to the issuer, an investor comes with
a specific requirement - a particular size, tenor or structure - and the issuer draws it privately under its MTN
programme. No bookbuild, no public announcement, no league table entry.
For the issuer it's opportunistic funding between public transactions, often on attractive terms because the
investor has a specific need. For the bank it's intermediation rather than execution.
rubric: Investor-initiated: a specific size, tenor or structure comes to the issuer
Drawn privately under the MTN programme, with no bookbuild or public announcement
Notes there is no league table credit
Frames it as opportunistic funding between public transactions
mistakes: Not knowing that it produces no league table entry, which is why it is invisible from the outside.

items.q: What is a Schuldschein?
items.a:
Legally it is a loan under German law, not a security - the Schuldschein itself is only the
evidencing certificate. It is transferred by assignment, not through a clearing system. Economically, though, it
behaves like a bond: standardised documentation, an arranging bookrunner, a broad institutional investor base and
an orderly placement process.
The shortest description I find accurate: a loan with capital-markets-style distribution.
rubric: States it is legally a loan under German law, not a security
Notes transfer is by assignment, not through a clearing system
Notes it behaves economically like a bond: standardised docs, an arranger, institutional distribution
mistakes: Calling it 'a private bond'. The legal characterisation is the foundation of the accounting, the absence of a prospectus and the absence of a secondary market.

items.q: SSD vs bond - the key differences?
items.a:
- Feature | Schuldschein | Benchmark bond
- Legal nature | loan (German law) | security
- Rating | usually none required | effectively required
- Documentation | c. 20-30 pages | prospectus, several hundred pages
- Size | from c. €20m, typically €50-200m | benchmark from €500m
- Tenors | typically 3-10 years, several in parallel | one per tranche
- Format | fixed and floating in parallel | one variant per tranche
- Process | several weeks | intraday
- Investor accounting | amortised cost (HGB) | mark to market
- Secondary market | effectively none | liquid
- Publicity | discreet | public
rubric: Legal nature: loan versus security
Rating usually not required versus effectively required
Documentation of 20-30 pages versus a full prospectus
Size from about 20m versus benchmark from 500m, and weeks of process versus intraday
Investor accounting at amortised cost versus mark to market
mistakes: Getting the size and process rows the wrong way round.

items.q: Why do investors buy Schuldscheine?
items.a:
The decisive point is the accounting. Because the Schuldschein is a loan and not a security,
German investors - particularly savings banks, cooperative banks and insurers - carry it at amortised cost under
HGB rather than at market value. Which means: spread widening doesn't flow through the P&L.
Two things follow. First, the investor is structurally a holder, not a trader. And second, the market is far less
sensitive to daily volatility - in a week when nobody can print a benchmark bond, Schuldschein processes simply
continue.
In exchange the investor accepts illiquidity and the absence of a rating, and gets paid for it in the spread.
rubric: Names the accounting as the decisive point: amortised cost under HGB, not market value
Concludes spread widening does not flow through the investor's P&L
Draws the two consequences: the investor is structurally a holder, and the market is insensitive to daily volatility
Notes the investor is paid for illiquidity and the absence of a rating
mistakes: Answering 'for the yield'. The accounting treatment explains the entire market.

items.q: Who is the SSD investor base?
items.a:
The core is German savings banks and cooperative banks, plus Landesbanken. Beyond that insurers and
pension vehicles, some asset managers, and for larger, better-known names increasingly Asian banks looking for
European corporate credit risk.
What they have in common is that they do their own credit analysis and don't need an external rating - and that
they want to hold.
rubric: Core is German savings banks, cooperative banks and Landesbanken
Adds insurers, pension vehicles and some asset managers
Notes Asian banks for larger names
Names the common feature: they do their own credit work and want to hold
mistakes: Describing it as a fund investor base. It is largely a bank investor base.

items.q: How does the SSD process work?
items.a:
Much slower and paced completely differently from a bond. Roughly: preparation with the issuer - 
documentation, financials, credit story, a structure proposal with tenors and formats. Then launch, sending
the materials to a broad investor list with an indicative spread range per tranche.
After that a marketing phase over several weeks, during which investors do their own credit analysis and
come back with questions. There's a subscription period rather than an intraday book. If demand is strong the
spread is tightened or the volume increased - that's called upsizing.
Finally allocation, documentation and drawdown.
So the core difference is: on a bond the binding constraint is the market window; on a Schuldschein it's the
investors' credit analysis. Which is why timing risk on a Schuldschein is far lower.
rubric: Preparation with the issuer: documentation, financials, credit story, structure proposal
Launch to a broad investor list with an indicative spread range per tranche
A marketing and subscription phase over weeks, not an intraday book, with upsizing if demand is strong
Names the core contrast: a bond's binding constraint is the market window, an SSD's is the investors' credit analysis
mistakes: Describing it as a slow bookbuild. The constraint is different in kind, not just in speed.

items.q: Why is an SSD tranched?
items.a:
Because the investor base is heterogeneous and you want to serve it in one process. A typical
Schuldschein comes with several tenors in parallel - say 3, 5, 7 and 10 years - each in a fixed and a floating
version against 6M Euribor. The investor self-selects whatever fits its book.
For the issuer that means: it smooths its maturity profile in a single transaction and mixes fixed and floating
without having to swap separately. A bond gives it exactly one tenor and one format per tranche.
In the current environment, with high rate volatility, the floating portion is a genuine argument.
rubric: Serves a heterogeneous investor base in one process
Several tenors in parallel, each in fixed and floating against 6M Euribor, with investors self-selecting
For the issuer: smooths the maturity profile and mixes fixed and floating without a separate swap
mistakes: Not connecting it to the floater logic: investors who do not want rate risk take the floating tranche.

items.q: SSD documentation and covenants?
items.a:
Short and standardised - usually twenty to thirty pages, mostly German law, sometimes English. No
prospectus, no prospectus liability, no exchange listing.
The covenant package is light: pari passu, negative pledge, change of control, occasionally a financial covenant
such as a leverage cap - the latter more for weaker credit profiles. Cross-default is standard.
The advantage for the issuer is time and cost; the price is that it serves an investor base that has to do the
credit analysis itself and needs information and time for that.
rubric: Twenty to thirty pages, mostly German law, no prospectus and no prospectus liability, no listing
Light covenant package: pari passu, negative pledge, change of control, cross-default
Occasionally a financial covenant such as a leverage cap, more for weaker credits
Names the trade: time and cost for the issuer, against an investor base that needs information and time
mistakes: Assuming an SSD is more restrictive than a bond. An IG bond's package is lighter still; the SSD is more negotiable, not tighter.

items.q: When SSD, when bond?
items.a:
I'd frame it as a decision tree, not a preference.
Schuldschein when: the issuer has no rating or doesn't want one; the size needed is below benchmark scale;
discretion and light documentation matter; several tenors and both formats are needed in one go; or it's a
first-time issuer stepping out of the classic bank loan market for the first time.
Bond when: the issuer is rated and achieves a lower all-in cost through size; it wants a visible, liquid
curve as a reference for future issuance; it needs €500m or more; or it intends to be a repeat issuer and wants to
cultivate a broad institutional investor base.
And the nuance: it isn't either-or. Large corporates use both - bonds for size and curve, Schuldschein for
tenor flexibility, investor diversification and less timing risk. On this desk both sit at one table, which is
exactly why the role interests me.
rubric: Frames it as a decision tree, not a preference
SSD when: no rating or no wish for one, sub-benchmark size, discretion, multiple tenors and formats, first-time issuer
Bond when: rated, needs size, wants a visible liquid curve, intends to be a repeat issuer
Notes it is not either-or: large corporates use both
mistakes: Presenting it as a ranking of products rather than a fit to the issuer's situation.

items.q: How do you price an SSD without a rating?
items.a:
Through a shadow rating and through comparable transactions. The arranger does an internal credit
analysis and places the issuer in a rating band - say 'BBB-like'. Then you look at where Schuldscheine of comparable
issuers have priced over recent months, by credit quality, sector, size and tenor.
What the issuer pays in the bank loan market often serves as the floor, and what a rated bond would cost as the
ceiling - the Schuldschein typically sits in between, with a premium for illiquidity and the absence of a rating.
And the process itself generates information: you start with a range per tranche and see during the subscription
phase where demand actually is. That's slower but more honest price discovery than an intraday book.
rubric: Uses a shadow rating from the arranger's internal credit analysis
Looks at where comparable SSDs have priced by credit quality, sector, size and tenor
Brackets it: the bank loan market as the floor, a rated bond as the ceiling
Notes the subscription phase itself generates price discovery, slower but more honest than an intraday book
mistakes: Claiming it cannot be priced without a rating.

items.q: What is a registered bond (Namensschuldverschreibung)?
items.a:
A note issued in the name of the holder rather than to bearer - it doesn't sit in clearing and isn't
freely tradeable, but is transferred by assignment.
The natural buyers are insurers and pension funds: again because of amortised cost accounting, and because the
instrument fits their regulatory investment framework. Typically very long tenors, because that's exactly where the
insurers' need is and where the public market delivers little.
For the issuer it is therefore a tool for long maturities in sizes that don't justify a benchmark.
rubric: A note issued in the holder's name, not to bearer, outside clearing, transferred by assignment
Names insurers and pension funds as the natural buyers, again for amortised cost and regulatory fit
Notes typically very long tenors, where the public market delivers little
mistakes: Confusing it with a Schuldschein. Both are non-securities, but the NSV is aimed at very long insurer money.

items.q: What is an MTN private placement?
items.a:
A bespoke drawdown under an issuer's EMTN programme, usually driven by reverse enquiry: an investor
comes with a specific size, tenor or structure, and the issuer prices it privately. No bookbuild, no public
announcement, no league table headline.
Fast, quiet, and the way issuers pick up opportunistic funding between public transactions. In practice it's the
tool you reach for when a client needs €80m for eleven years - a size and tenor no benchmark bond can serve.
rubric: A bespoke drawdown under the issuer's EMTN programme
Usually driven by reverse enquiry from an investor with a specific need
No bookbuild, no public announcement, no league table headline
Names the use case: a size and tenor no benchmark bond can serve
mistakes: Confusing it with a Schuldschein. The MTN PP is a security under a programme; the SSD is a loan.

items.q: How big is the SSD market?
items.a:
In 2025 new volume was around €25bn - the fifth-highest year in the market's history and above the prior
year, across more than a hundred transactions with an average size in the region of €200m. Issuers from around
twelve sectors and eleven countries.
For 2026 the houses' forecasts point to a similar order of magnitude again, driven mainly by refinancing from
unrated issuers - rated companies continue to enjoy a cost advantage in the public bond market.
ESG-linked Schuldscheine run at around a tenth of volume, though the sustainability link is rarely fixed
contractually - it feeds more into the credit analysis.
rubric: Gives annual new volume in the right order of magnitude
Notes the driver is refinancing from unrated issuers, since rated names have a cost advantage in the public market
Notes ESG-linked SSDs are a modest share and the link is rarely fixed contractually
mistakes: Quoting a volume figure without a year attached.

items.q: What are the drawbacks of an SSD?
items.a:
For the issuer: no visible curve, so no reference price for later transactions; limited scalability,
because the investor base is narrower than in the public market; and the process takes weeks, which is a
disadvantage if funding need is acute.
For the investor: no liquidity - anyone who wants to sell has a problem - no external rating, so the full
analytical burden, and less transparency in ongoing monitoring.
And a structural point: in a credit crisis, a market where nobody marks to market and nobody can sell is very
quiet - until it isn't. Prices adjust with a lag.
rubric: For the issuer: no visible curve, limited scalability, a process that takes weeks
For the investor: no liquidity, no external rating, less transparency in monitoring
Makes the structural point: amortised cost suppresses reported volatility, not actual credit risk
mistakes: Listing only issuer drawbacks and missing that prices adjust with a lag in a credit crisis.

items.q: What is a corporate hybrid?
items.a:
A deeply subordinated, generally perpetual bond issued by a non-financial company that combines debt
and equity features. Typical characteristics: no fixed maturity date, ranking only just above equity, an issuer call
right after typically five or seven years, a coupon reset at the call date, and the issuer's right to defer the
coupon - usually cumulatively, so it has to be paid later.
The point of the structure is that rating agencies grant it partial equity character.
rubric: Deeply subordinated, generally perpetual, issued by a non-financial company
Names the features: no fixed maturity, ranks just above equity, issuer call after typically 5 or 7 years
Names the coupon reset at call and the right to defer coupons, usually cumulatively
States the point of the structure: partial equity treatment from the rating agencies
mistakes: Confusing a corporate hybrid with a bank AT1. The bank instrument has a write-down or conversion trigger; the corporate one does not.

items.q: Equity credit - why issue a hybrid?
items.a:
Rating agencies count a correctly structured hybrid - at S&P generally 50% - as equity. Which means:
of a €500m issue, only €250m feeds into the leverage metrics.
The benefit to the issuer is therefore clear: it strengthens its credit metrics and defends its rating
without diluting existing shareholders. Typical triggers are a large acquisition, a capex programme - for
instance at utilities and grid operators - or pressure from a rating agency.
The price is a materially higher coupon than senior unsecured, because the investor bears subordination,
deferral risk and extension risk. You are buying rating capital, and it costs.
rubric: Rating agencies count a correctly structured hybrid as part equity, typically 50% at S&P
Works the arithmetic: half of the issue does not feed the leverage metrics
Names the benefit: defends the rating without diluting shareholders
Names the price: a materially higher coupon for subordination, deferral and extension risk
mistakes: Missing the dilution point, which is the reason a CFO picks a hybrid over an equity raise.

items.q: Explain the hybrid structure.
items.a:
Typically 'NC5' or 'NC7' - non-callable for five or seven years respectively. At the first call date the
issuer has the right to call at par. If it doesn't call, the coupon resets, usually as the mid-swap rate for the
reset period plus the original margin.
On top of that come step-ups: a small one - often 25 basis points - after around ten years, and a larger one - 
often 75 basis points - after around twenty or twenty-five. They are deliberately calibrated to create an economic
incentive to call without giving the bond a legal fixed maturity, which would destroy the equity character.
That's why the market calculates and trades hybrids to the first call, not to perpetuity: yield is
yield-to-call, duration is duration to call.
rubric: NC5 or NC7: non-callable for five or seven years, then callable at par
At the call date the coupon resets to mid-swaps for the reset period plus the original margin
Names the step-ups and their sizes and timing
Explains the design logic: big enough to incentivise a call, small enough not to be a legal maturity that would destroy equity credit
Notes the market trades hybrids to first call: yield-to-call and duration-to-call
mistakes: Treating the perpetual maturity as real. The market prices to first call.

items.q: What is extension risk?
items.a:
The risk that the issuer doesn't call at the first call date. The market prices hybrids as though they
will be called - if that isn't confirmed, the effective maturity extends abruptly, duration jumps, and the price
falls accordingly.
Economically an issuer doesn't call when refinancing would be more expensive than the reset coupon. That was a
real issue during the period of sharply rising rates.
In practice, though, reputation matters a great deal: an issuer who fails to call once pays permanently more on
its next hybrid and may find no market at all. Which is why most investment grade issuers call even when it's
marginal on pure arithmetic.
rubric: The risk that the issuer does not call at the first call date
Explains the price effect: effective maturity extends abruptly, duration jumps, price falls
Gives the economic condition: an issuer does not call when refinancing costs more than the reset coupon
Names the reputational constraint that makes most IG issuers call anyway
mistakes: Giving only the arithmetic. The repeated-game reputational cost is why marginal calls still happen.

items.q: How do you price a hybrid?
items.a:
The starting point is the same issuer's senior curve at the tenor to the first call. On top of that
comes a subordination premium, which depending on the issuer and the market phase can be a multiple of the senior
spread - often broadly in the region of two to three times, but it varies a lot.
You sanity-check that against other hybrids: the issuer's own outstanding hybrids and hybrids of comparable
names, each measured as the premium over their own senior curve. That premium is the actual comparison metric, not
the absolute spread.
And the new issue premium on hybrids is systematically higher than on senior - the structure is more complex and
the investor base narrower.
rubric: Starts from the issuer's own senior curve at the tenor to first call
Adds a subordination premium, given as a rough range and flagged as variable
Sanity-checks against other hybrids measured as the premium over their own senior curve, not the absolute spread
Notes the new issue premium on hybrids is systematically higher than on senior
mistakes: Comparing absolute hybrid spreads across issuers. The premium over each issuer's own senior curve is the comparable.

items.q: How do rating agencies treat a hybrid?
items.a:
Two effects. First the equity credit on the metrics side - at S&P typically 50%, provided the
structure meets the criteria: sufficient subordination, deferral capability, adequate effective maturity.
Second the instrument rating itself: the hybrid is notched down from the issuer rating - usually by two notches
for an investment grade issuer, more for weaker profiles. That reflects subordination and deferral risk.
And the equity credit isn't necessarily permanent: if the structure no longer meets the criteria it can fall
away - which removes the entire purpose of the issue for the issuer and can itself be grounds for a call.
rubric: Equity credit on the metrics side, typically 50% at S&P, subject to structural criteria
Instrument notching: usually two notches below the issuer rating for an IG name, more for weaker profiles
Notes equity credit is not permanent and can fall away if criteria change
Knows a rating methodology event call exists for exactly that case
mistakes: Conflating the equity credit with the instrument rating. They are two separate effects.

items.q: Who buys hybrids?
items.a:
Mainly specialist funds - hybrid and subordinated debt funds - insurers reaching for yield, and
crossover investors: investment grade houses that get a high-yield-like coupon through the hybrid of a solid IG
issuer, but with credit risk they already know.
That's precisely the appeal and the risk at once: you're buying the credit risk of an A or BBB name, but with the
price volatility of a subordinated instrument.
rubric: Specialist hybrid and subordinated debt funds
Insurers reaching for yield
Crossover buyers: IG accounts taking a high-yield-like coupon on credit they already know
Names the framing: IG credit risk with subordinated price behaviour
mistakes: Missing why hybrids sell off harder than their credit quality suggests in a risk-off move.

items.q: Give me the rating scale.
items.a:
- S&P / Fitch | Moody's | Band
- AAA | Aaa | Investment Grade
- AA+ / AA / AA− | Aa1 / Aa2 / Aa3 | Investment Grade
- A+ / A / A− | A1 / A2 / A3 | Investment Grade
- BBB+ / BBB / BBB− | Baa1 / Baa2 / Baa3 | Investment Grade
- BB+ / BB / BB− | Ba1 / Ba2 / Ba3 | High Yield
- B+ / B / B− | B1 / B2 / B3 | High Yield
- CCC+ / CCC / CCC− | Caa1 / Caa2 / Caa3 | High Yield
- CC / C / D | Ca / C | High Yield

The line: BBB− / Baa3 is the lowest investment grade notch; BB+ / Ba1 is the highest high yield notch.
rubric: Gives the S&P/Fitch and Moody's scales side by side down to at least CCC
Names BBB- / Baa3 as the lowest investment grade notch and BB+ / Ba1 as the highest high yield notch
Knows the modifier convention: +/- for S&P and Fitch, 1/2/3 for Moody's, with 1 strongest
mistakes: Getting Moody's modifier direction wrong, or putting a modifier on AAA.

items.q: Why does the IG/HY line matter so much?
items.a:
Because it's a demand cliff, not a gradual deterioration. A great many institutional mandates - 
insurers, pension funds, index funds - may only hold investment grade. If an issuer falls from BBB− to BB+, those
investors have to sell regardless of what they think of the credit. That's called a fallen angel.
The consequence is a spread jump far larger than the single notch justifies economically. In reverse there's the
rising star.
For the issuer that means: defending the BBB− is one of the most important funding decisions there is - and one
of the main reasons hybrids get issued.
rubric: Explains it as a demand cliff, not a gradual deterioration
Names the mandate constraint: many institutional mandates may only hold investment grade
Names the fallen angel and the forced selling that follows
Notes the spread jump is far larger than one notch justifies, and loops to why hybrids get issued
mistakes: Treating the boundary as one more notch. It is a discontinuity in the buyer base.

items.q: Outlook vs watchlist?
items.a:
An outlook is the medium-term directional assessment - positive, stable or negative - over
typically one to two years. A CreditWatch or review is short-term and event-driven: the agency signals that
it will decide within roughly ninety days, usually triggered by an acquisition, a disposal or an event.
Practically that means: a watch moves spreads much more than an outlook change, because concrete action is in
sight.
rubric: Outlook is a medium-term directional view over one to two years
CreditWatch or review is short-term and event-driven, with a decision expected in about ninety days
Notes a watch moves spreads much more than an outlook change, because action is in sight
mistakes: Treating the two as interchangeable degrees of the same signal.

items.q: Which credit metrics do you look at?
items.a:
I'd structure it in four blocks:
Leverage: net debt to EBITDA. As a rough orientation, investment grade often sits below 3x, but that's
heavily sector-dependent - a regulated utility carries 5x comfortably, a cyclical is already stretched at 3x.
Coverage: EBITDA or EBIT to interest expense. The higher the safer; in IG typically above 4x to 5x. That
metric has become more important in the current rate environment, because refinancing happens at materially higher
coupons.
Cash flow: free cash flow and FFO to net debt - S&P works heavily with FFO/debt. That matters more to
me than EBITDA, because it accounts for working capital and capex.
Maturity profile and liquidity: what falls due when, which facilities are committed and undrawn, how much
cash is on hand.
rubric: Leverage: net debt to EBITDA, with an explicit sector caveat rather than a hard threshold
Coverage: EBITDA or EBIT to interest, and why it matters more at higher refinancing coupons
Cash flow: free cash flow and FFO to debt, naming FFO/debt as S&P's anchor
Maturity profile and liquidity: what falls due when, committed undrawn facilities, cash on hand
mistakes: Quoting 'below 3.0x for IG' as a hard rule. It invites an immediate counterexample from a regulated utility.

items.q: Why can EBITDA mislead?
items.a:
Because it excludes capex, working capital, interest and tax - in other words practically everything
debt is actually serviced from. A capital-intensive company with high EBITDA can still have persistently negative
free cash flow.
On top of that, 'adjusted EBITDA' is definition-dependent. On my waste management mandate we did exactly that: we
isolated three opex lines to justify the normalisation. It was methodologically well grounded - but it also shows
how much latitude sits in the metric.
For a bondholder, free cash flow after capex is therefore the more honest measure.
rubric: EBITDA excludes capex, working capital, interest and tax, which is what debt is serviced from
Gives the case: a capital-intensive company with high EBITDA and persistently negative free cash flow
Notes adjusted EBITDA is definition-dependent and shows how much latitude sits in the add-backs
Concludes free cash flow after capex is the more honest bondholder measure
mistakes: Criticising EBITDA in the abstract with no concrete case where it misleads.

items.q: Incurrence vs maintenance covenants?
items.a:
A maintenance covenant has to be complied with on an ongoing basis - typically tested quarterly,
for instance a leverage cap. A breach gives a termination right even if the company hasn't done anything. That's
classic bank loan logic.
An incurrence covenant only bites when the company actively does something - takes on new debt, pays
dividends, sells assets. That's bond logic, particularly in high yield.
Investment grade bonds generally have no financial covenants at all - there the investor relies on the rating and
on negative pledge, pari passu and a change-of-control put. That's the price of credit quality: a BBB issuer gets
light documentation, a B issuer doesn't.
rubric: Maintenance: tested on an ongoing basis, typically quarterly; a breach gives a termination right without any action by the company
Incurrence: bites only when the company does something, such as raising debt, paying dividends or selling assets
Gives the three-tier picture: bank loan, then high yield bond, then IG bond with no financial covenants at all
Notes the IG investor relies on the rating, negative pledge, pari passu and a change-of-control put
mistakes: Listing the two definitions without connecting covenant strength to credit quality.

items.q: Negative pledge? Structural subordination?
items.a:
Negative pledge: the issuer's undertaking not to grant security over assets to other creditors
without treating bondholders equally. It protects unsecured creditors from being subordinated after the fact to
newly secured ones.
Structural subordination: if the bond is issued by the holding company but the assets and operating cash
flow sit in subsidiaries, the holdco creditor ranks behind all creditors of the subsidiary in insolvency. He only
gets what flows up as a dividend after the subsidiary level has been served.
The remedy is guarantees from the operating subsidiaries - which is why 'who is the issuer and who guarantees' is
one of the first questions on any transaction.
rubric: Negative pledge: an undertaking not to grant security to others without equal treatment of bondholders
Structural subordination: a holdco creditor ranks behind all creditors of the operating subsidiaries
Explains the mechanism: the holdco only gets what flows up as a dividend after the subsidiary level is served
Names the remedy: guarantees from the operating subsidiaries
mistakes: Confusing structural with contractual subordination. Structural comes from where the assets sit, not from the documents.

items.q: How would you assess a company as a credit analyst?
items.a:
Top down, and with the opposite sign to equity analysis.
Business risk: how stable and predictable is the cash flow? How cyclical is the sector? How strong is the
market position, how good is pricing power? Regulated or contracted revenues are worth more to me than growth.
Financial risk: leverage, coverage, cash generation, maturity profile, liquidity reserves. S&P combines
exactly those two axes in a matrix to get the anchor rating.
