Modifiers: financial policy - what has management historically done with surplus cash? Shareholder
structure, M&A appetite, commitment to the rating.
And the downside question: what happens in a bad scenario? If revenue falls twenty percent, does interest
coverage become critical? As a bondholder my upside is capped at coupon and principal - so what interests me isn't
the best case, it's the worst case that is still plausible.
rubric: Business risk: cash flow stability and predictability, cyclicality, market position, pricing power
Financial risk: leverage, coverage, cash generation, maturity profile, liquidity
Names the agency matrix that combines the two into an anchor rating
Modifiers: financial policy, shareholder structure, M&A appetite, commitment to the rating
Ends on the downside question, because the bondholder's upside is capped
mistakes: Running an equity analysis with the sign flipped. Growth is worth less to a creditor than contracted revenue.

items.q: Good for equity, bad for credit - how?
items.a:
Very often, in fact. A debt-funded share buyback is good for the shareholder - fewer shares, higher
earnings per share - and bad for the bondholder: more debt on the same cash flow.
The same goes for a large debt-funded acquisition, for aggressive dividend policy, or for a spin-off that
separates the stable part of the business out of the credit group.
The underlying conflict is always the same: the shareholder has unlimited upside and benefits from risk, the
creditor doesn't. That's why covenants exist - and why the change-of-control put is so widespread in bonds.
rubric: Gives the debt-funded buyback as the cleanest case: good for EPS, bad for leverage on the same cash flow
Adds debt-funded acquisitions, aggressive dividends, and spin-offs that remove stable cash flow from the credit group
Names the underlying conflict: the shareholder has unlimited upside and benefits from risk, the creditor does not
Connects it to why covenants and change-of-control puts exist
mistakes: Not having a concrete case ready. This question tests whether the valuation instinct has actually been reoriented.

items.q: Where are ECB rates?
items.a:
Deposit facility 2.25%, main refinancing operations 2.40%, marginal lending 2.65%.
The ECB hiked by 25 basis points on 11 June - the first increase in almost three years - and
held on 23 July. The Council remains explicitly data-dependent and won't commit to a rate path. APP and PEPP
continue to run down, with no reinvestment of maturing principal.
rubric: Gives the deposit facility rate, the main refinancing rate and the marginal lending rate
States the direction and date of the most recent decision
Notes whether the Council is committing to a path or staying data-dependent
mistakes: Quoting a rate without knowing when it was last changed.

items.q: Why did the ECB hike?
items.a:
Because of energy, not demand. The Middle East conflict and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz
pushed oil and gas sharply higher. The market then repriced inflation risk far more than growth risk.
In July the ECB made clear that energy prices remain highly volatile, sit above pre-conflict levels, and that the
full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to play out. What it is watching particularly are second-round
effects - that is, whether the energy shock embeds itself in wages and services prices.
rubric: Identifies the driver as a supply-side energy shock rather than demand
Names second-round effects into wages and services as the actual policy question
Explains why a supply shock is the worst case: inflation up and growth down at once
mistakes: Explaining a hike with demand-side reasoning when the driver was energy.

items.q: Where is inflation?
items.a:
The euro area was at 2.9% in July, up from 2.8% in June - so rising again, and above target since
the spring.
The composition is what matters: energy up 10.0% against 8.5% in June, services 3.3%, non-energy
industrial goods only 0.9%, food 1.2%. Excluding energy the rate is 2.2%.
Which means: the upward pressure comes almost entirely from energy. The core is close to target - but services
inflation at 3.3% is the number that keeps the ECB awake, because that's where second-round effects would show.
rubric: Gives the headline euro area rate and the direction of travel
Breaks it into energy, services, non-energy industrial goods and food
Identifies services inflation as the number that matters for second-round effects
mistakes: Quoting a 'core' figure without saying which definition, since core definitions vary.

items.q: Where is the 10y Bund?
items.a:
Around 3.16%, as of yesterday. In July it was briefly above 3.2%, the highest in about fifteen
years; it has come back slightly since, because there's been some movement at the negotiating table on the Strait of
Hormuz. Roughly 40 basis points higher than a year ago.
Two drivers: inflation and rate expectations, and - very substantially - supply. Germany is running record
issuance to fund infrastructure and defence, while the ECB no longer reinvests - so private investors have to
absorb a record net volume.
rubric: Gives the 10y Bund level and how it has moved over the month and year
Names the two drivers: inflation and rate expectations, and supply
Explains the supply side: record German issuance while the ECB no longer reinvests
mistakes: Quoting a level from memory that is a week old. This moves daily.

items.q: What is the Fed doing?
items.a:
The Fed held on 29 July, with a target range of 3.50% to 3.75% - with several dissents; it
was a contested meeting. The chair since this year is Kevin Warsh, who succeeded Jerome Powell.
Warsh has visibly stepped back from forward guidance and set up several internal task forces, including on
communications, the balance sheet and the inflation framework. The market expectation is that the Fed pauses for the
rest of the year.
That matters for the EUR market because the rate differential and the cross-currency basis determine whether an
issuer funds more cheaply in EUR or USD.
rubric: Gives the target range and the date and outcome of the most recent meeting
Names the current chair
Explains why it matters for EUR: the rate differential and cross-currency basis drive EUR versus USD issuance
mistakes: Treating the Fed as background. The divergence is what drives the issuance arbitrage.

items.q: How is the Middle East conflict affecting bonds?
items.a:
Through three channels.
Energy and inflation: the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has pushed oil sharply higher - Brent is
around a third above where it was a year ago and has traded above $100 at points. That drives inflation, pushes
central banks towards tightening and therefore lifts the whole level of yields. That's the most important channel,
and it works against bonds, not for them.
Risk aversion: in acute escalations there is a flight to quality - Bunds and Treasuries bid, credit
spreads wider. European IG spreads widened noticeably in the spring for that reason and have largely retraced since.
Volatility and issuance windows: that's the channel that affects us most directly. High rate volatility
makes investors more price sensitive, books get thinner, new issue premiums rise - in July to the highest level of
the year - and windows narrow. Issuers are currently accepting the higher premium rather than waiting.
The interesting point is that secondary spreads don't reflect any of this: they're historically tight. The stress
shows up in the primary market, not in the secondary market.
rubric: Channel one, energy and inflation: higher oil lifts the whole level of yields and works against bonds
Channel two, risk aversion: flight to quality bids govvies and widens credit spreads
Channel three, volatility and windows: thinner books, higher new issue premiums, narrower windows
States explicitly that the inflation channel dominates the flight-to-quality channel
Notes the stress shows up in the primary market, not in secondary spreads
mistakes: The naive answer: 'conflict means flight to quality means bonds rally'. The rate channel dominates.

items.q: Oil and the transmission to a corporate bond?
items.a:
Brent is around $88 to $89, comfortably a third above a year ago, with very high volatility - above $100
at points, then back below $85, depending on the state of negotiations.
The chain through to a corporate bond: oil up → inflation up → central bank tightens or pauses for longer →
reference rate up → bond price falls, regardless of the credit. That's the dominant effect.
On top of that a credit channel, but a differentiated one: for energy-intensive industry, chemicals and transport
input costs rise and margins come under pressure - spreads widen there. For oil and gas producers it's the reverse.
For regulated utilities it's largely passed through.
And the third effect is on issuance activity itself: higher volatility, thinner books, higher premiums.
rubric: Gives the oil level and the year-on-year move
Runs the chain: oil up, inflation up, central bank tighter, reference rate up, bond price down regardless of credit
Differentiates the credit channel by sector: energy-intensive industry hurt, producers helped, regulated utilities pass through
Names the third effect on issuance activity itself
mistakes: Saying 'spreads widen' undifferentiated. The sector split is what makes it an analyst answer.

items.q: What does ECB QT mean for spreads?
items.a:
APP and PEPP continue to run down, with no reinvestment of redemptions. That structurally removes a very
large, price-insensitive buyer from the market - the ECB also bought corporate bonds under the CSPP.
Two consequences. First, the private sector has to absorb a materially higher net volume, in both government and
corporate bonds. Second - and I think this matters more - the market is now more sensitive again to supply and to
flows, because the buffer is gone. A supply pile-up in one week feeds through to premiums more strongly today than
it did during the purchase programmes.
rubric: Names the runoff of APP and PEPP with no reinvestment of redemptions
Identifies the key concept: a large price-insensitive buyer has been removed
Consequence one: the private sector absorbs a higher net volume
Consequence two, and the more important one: the market is more sensitive to supply and flows, so a supply pile-up feeds through to premiums
mistakes: Framing QT purely as volume. It was that the ECB bought regardless of price.

items.q: What are primary market conditions like right now?
items.a:
Two-tier, and that's the interesting part.
Secondary, spreads are historically tight. The European high yield index is around 260 basis points and has
tightened further recently; IG correspondingly tight. Measured against its own history, credit is expensive.
Primary is less comfortable. Average new issue premiums rose in July to the highest level of the year,
books have thinned, and investors are visibly more price sensitive - driven by rate volatility and the Middle East
situation, not by credit concerns.
My reading would be: the investor is currently being paid by the rate, not by the credit risk premium. All-in
yields are attractive, spreads are not. And that's why execution is more demanding even though the index levels look
good.
Seasonally, August is dead anyway; the second half starts in September and then runs hard into late November.
rubric: Describes the market as two-tier
Secondary: spreads historically tight, credit expensive against its own history
Primary: new issue premiums up, books thinner, investors more price sensitive, driven by rate volatility not credit
Draws the conclusion: the investor is paid by the rate, not by the credit risk premium
mistakes: Reading the tight index level as an easy market. Execution is where the stress is.

items.q: What's the biggest risk to the market right now?
items.a:
I'd name two, and I think the second is underrated.
First, a renewed escalation around the Strait of Hormuz. Negotiations are running but they're stalling. A
failure would mean oil materially higher, inflation expectations higher, central banks more restrictive - and this
time without the buffer that a low level of yields used to provide.
Second, valuation in credit itself. Spreads are tight, measured against their own history very tight, and
they price in little tolerance for error. If a shock came - macro or idiosyncratic - the path down is longer than
the path up. That's not a forecast, but it is an asymmetry.
What I don't see as an acute risk is credit quality itself: the stress at the moment is in execution and in
premiums, not in defaults or downgrades.
rubric: Names an identifiable macro escalation risk with the transmission spelled out
Names credit valuation itself: tight spreads price in little tolerance for error
Frames it as an asymmetry rather than a forecast
Distinguishes what is stressed (execution, concessions) from what is not (defaults, downgrades)
mistakes: Forecasting. 'That is not a prediction, it is an asymmetry' is the right register for a candidate.

items.q: Why does November matter?
items.a:
Because the second half of the year is compressed in the primary market. August is seasonally
effectively dead - many investors aren't staffed and nobody wants to issue into a thin book. From September the
market reopens and then runs very densely until late November, because after that the year-end comes: from December
investors' books close, balance sheet dates approach, and nobody issues unless they have to.
Which means: anyone who still wants to fund in Q4 has to do it in October and November.
rubric: August is seasonally dead: investors unstaffed, nobody issues into a thin book
September reopens and the market runs densely until late November
From December books close and balance sheet dates approach
Concludes anyone funding in Q4 has to do it in October and November
mistakes: Not knowing the calendar of the job you are applying to.

items.q: Who issues EM EUR, and why euro?
items.a:
Typically companies from central and eastern Europe - Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Romania, Slovakia - 
plus Turkish and occasionally Middle Eastern names choosing euros over dollars.
The reasons: natural currency matching, because a large part of revenues, cost base or acquisition targets
is in euros; a European investor base that knows the region; and depending on the cross-currency basis,
simply cheaper all-in cost than in dollars.
rubric: Names CEE corporates, plus Turkish and occasionally Middle Eastern issuers
Currency matching: revenues, cost base or acquisition targets in euros
A European investor base that knows the region
Cross-currency basis can make EUR cheaper all-in than USD
mistakes: Assuming EM issuance in EUR is only about diversification. Currency matching usually comes first.

items.q: How does EM execution differ?
items.a:
In five respects. Format - usually Reg S only, to avoid the disclosure and liability burden of a
US distribution; that limits the buyer base to Europe and Asia. Investor base - dedicated EM credit funds
plus crossover buyers, i.e. European IG accounts reaching for yield in BBB and BB names. Price - wider
spreads and systematically higher new issue premiums. Book - more price sensitive, less granular, more
dependent on a few large accounts. Windows - narrower, because EM issuance reacts far more strongly to risk
sentiment and rate volatility.
And structurally: the sovereign rating usually caps the corporate rating, which anchors the pricing conversation
from the outset.
rubric: Format: usually Reg S only, which limits the buyer base to Europe and Asia
Investor base: dedicated EM credit funds plus crossover buyers reaching for yield
Price: wider spreads and systematically higher new issue premiums
Book: more price sensitive, less granular, dependent on a few large accounts
Names the sovereign ceiling as the structural anchor on the rating and therefore the pricing
mistakes: Missing the sovereign ceiling, which anchors the pricing conversation from the outset.

items.q: Why is a bank with a regional branch network well placed in EM DCM?
items.a:
Because of the on-the-ground presence. A group with banks in the region is house bank to many of
these issuers - a lending relationship, the payments business and local credit knowledge - which means access
comes out of an existing relationship rather than out of a pitch from outside.
That also explains why a syndicate desk at such a house sees EM flow a purely domestic competitor does not.
rubric: Argues from structure: banks on the ground and house-bank relationships in the region
Notes access comes out of an existing lending relationship rather than a cold pitch
Explains the consequence: the desk sees EM flow a purely domestic house would not
mistakes: Arguing from adjectives rather than from structure.

items.q: Explain a bond to a 12-year-old.
items.a:
Imagine a company wants to build a new factory today and doesn't have the money. It asks a lot of people
to each lend it a bit. As a thank you it pays interest every year and gives the money back at the end.
The difference from a normal loan is: my claim is a kind of voucher that I can sell on. And because other people
can buy it, it has a price every day - and that price rises when the company is doing well, or when rates fall.
rubric: Explains lending to a company for interest and repayment, in plain language
Includes the tradability point, which is what makes it a bond
Resists adding technical detail once started
mistakes: Adding jargon halfway through. The discipline of staying simple is the test.

items.q: Duration of 6, rates +75bp - what happens?
items.a:
Roughly a 4.5% price loss - 6 times 0.75. Two refinements: because of positive convexity the actual loss
is slightly smaller than that linear approximation. And if the credit spread moves at the same time, that effect
comes on top via spread duration.
rubric: Gives the arithmetic first: roughly a 4.5% price loss, 6 times 0.75
Refines: positive convexity means the actual loss is slightly smaller than the linear approximation
Refines: a simultaneous spread move adds on top via spread duration
mistakes: Leading with the caveats. It sounds evasive; lead with the number, then refine.

items.q: 5y at MS+80, 10y at MS+110 - what does that tell you?
items.a:
That the credit curve is normally upward sloping, at 30 basis points over five years - the market
demands a premium for the additional tenor risk, which is plausible for a solid issuer.
For a new issue at seven years I'd interpolate linearly to roughly +92, then adjust slightly downwards because
credit curves typically flatten as tenor extends. So fair value somewhere around +90 to +92, plus new issue premium.
And I'd check whether both levels are actually tradeable - if the ten-year is a small, illiquid line, part of that
premium is liquidity and not credit curve.
rubric: Reads the curve: 30bp over five years is a normal upward-sloping credit curve
Interpolates to the target tenor and states the number
Adjusts downwards for credit curves flattening as tenor extends
Questions the data: checks whether both levels are actually tradeable, since an illiquid long line carries a liquidity premium not a credit premium
mistakes: Interpolating and stopping. Questioning the data quality is what a desk person does automatically.

items.q: The book is 6x covered at IPTs - what now?
items.a:
First: that's a signal it was launched too generously. I'd tighten substantially - considerably more
than a normal step - while watching two things: how much book is lost, and whether the large real money orders stay.
And I'd discuss size with the issuer: a six-times-covered book is also an opportunity to increase the volume
rather than pulling the whole advantage into the spread. Which is better depends on whether the issuer is optimising
for money or for price.
What I wouldn't do is go to the last basis point. If the bond trades worse the next day, it was expensively
bought.
rubric: Reads a 6x book at IPTs as a signal the deal was launched too generously
Tightens substantially, watching how much book is lost and whether large real money stays
Raises the upsize option and asks what the issuer is optimising for, money or price
Declines to go to the last basis point, because a worse break is expensively bought
mistakes: Only tightening. A heavily covered book is an opportunity on two axes, size as well as spread.

items.q: Issuer wants to print today into a shaky market.
items.a:
I'd break the question in two: does he have to today, or does he want to today? If a maturity is due or
an acquisition has to be funded, waiting isn't an option and the only question left is how to reduce the risk in
execution - more conservative IPTs, a more generous premium, possibly a shorter tenor or smaller size, and an anchor
investor to carry the book.
If he's issuing opportunistically, I'd advise waiting - but with one condition: you have to be able to say what
you're waiting for. 'For better conditions' isn't a plan. 'Until after the ECB meeting on Thursday' is.
And honestly: in the current environment many issuers would rather accept the higher premium than wait for a
window that may not come.
rubric: Splits the question: does the issuer have to print today, or want to
If it must: reduces execution risk with conservative IPTs, a more generous premium, possibly shorter tenor or smaller size, and an anchor order
If opportunistic: advises waiting, but only on condition you can name what you are waiting for
Notes 'for better conditions' is not a plan; 'until after Thursday's ECB meeting' is
mistakes: Advising to wait with no named event to wait for.

items.q: Tell me about a recent deal you followed.
items.a:
You need to be able to answer this with a concrete deal. Structure:
"Issuer X, rating, sector. They issued a [tenor] bond of [size]. IPTs were at mid-swaps plus [X], it priced at
plus [Y] - so [X−Y] basis points of tightening. The book was around [Z] times covered. What I found interesting was
[one concrete point: the premium relative to the environment / the tenor / the investor distribution / how it traded
the next day]."
rubric: Names a specific issuer, rating, sector, tenor and size
Gives IPT, final spread and therefore the tightening
Gives the book size or coverage
Adds one concrete observation: the premium relative to the environment, the investor distribution, or how it traded
mistakes: A deal you cannot give numbers for. Without IPT and final spread it is not a deal you followed.

items.q: If you had €1m, what bond would you buy?
items.a:
I'd break the question into two decisions: rates and credit.
On rates I'm currently cautious on long duration. The ECB has just hiked, the energy shock hasn't fully
worked through, and Bund supply is at record levels. I'd position more in the middle of the curve, five to seven
years.
On credit I'd say: spreads are tight, I'm not being paid particularly well for credit risk. So I'd take
quality - a solid BBB or A in a defensive sector with stable, ideally regulated cash flows - and take my return from
the all-in yield rather than from the spread.
So: mid part of the curve, high credit quality, return coming from the rate rather than the spread. And that's an
opinion, not a recommendation - I have no track record in fixed income.
rubric: Splits the answer into a rates decision and a credit decision
Takes a position on duration with a reason
Takes a position on credit quality with a reason, connected to where spreads are
Closes with an honest caveat about the absence of a track record
mistakes: Naming a security. The structure is the answer, not the bond.
